#3048. iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.

#3045. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3044. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

#3042. Jensen Huang Is Back at Nvidia. These Are 3 Remaining Concerns With Nvidia and What They Mean for the Stock.

Investors are breathing a sigh of relief, but Nvidia is not completely out of the woods.

By Will Healy – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:10PM EST

The return of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) is welcome news to shareholders. The stock was up more than 30% in early Monday trading as Huang's reinstatement removed a major source of uncertainty.

However, Huang's return creates new uncertainties or brings existing ones to light. Here are three concerns investors need to watch and whether Nvidia can prosper now that Huang is back.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Despite Huang's return, the board's probe goes on. The board appointed a committee comprised of independent directors to investigate the CEO's behavior and retained independent counsel to assist. This inquiry proceeds with Huang's approval.

Moreover, the federal government continues to review the matter. Although President Trump remained supportive of Huang, the FBI continues to investigate Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), whom a U.S. official linked to Chinese state security.

Additionally, the U.S. Congress is also conducting its own investigation. To that end, Jensen Huang will testify before congressional committees on Dec. 1.

Hence, while Nvidia's shareholders reacted well to the reinstatement, investors should remember he could still face repercussions for his behavior.

Furthermore, the current members of the board of directors likely face an uncertain future. As mentioned, the board continues to investigate Huang.

Unfortunately, the rush to judgment on Jensen Huang's fate could easily bring repercussions for the board itself.

Admittedly, boards tend to fire employees for having an inappropriate relationship with subordinates. Also, since its job is to focus on a company's affairs, the alleged affair with Nvidia's VP of healthcare, Kimberly Powell, is probably more concerning to them than the indiscretion with the alleged Chinese spy.

Nonetheless, the board is not legally required to terminate executives for such relationships. Moreover, it pressured Huang to resign even though the investigations had not been completed. Since the board lacked a succession plan, it made a move that created tremendous uncertainty for shareholders.

For now, no word has come down on the fate of various board members, but investors should probably be as watchful of their fate as they are of Jensen Huang's.

Jensen Huang's return also puts a spotlight on one of the concerns about his leadership: circular financing.

Huang and CFO Colette Kress have avoided using this term. However, as securing funding has become more difficult, the company has financially backstopped many of its customers. This included a $250 billion backstop for OpenAI that Kress negotiated down to $105 billion.

Concerns about OpenAI's financing have weighed on the stocks of partners such as Oracle (ORCL +12.34%). Also, longtime investors may also recall that circular financing devastated companies during the dot-com boom. At that time, Cisco (CSCO +6.80%) took a $2.25 billion write-down in 2001. Customer bankruptcies hit the company so hard that it traded below its all-time high for more than 25 years.

Nvidia's financial strength may help it avert a decades-long downturn. Nonetheless, similar customer bankruptcies could end the bull market in Nvidia stock.

Despite these concerns, Jensen Huang's return as CEO is, and will likely remain, bullish for Nvidia's shareholders.

Amid these worries, there is no obvious replacement for Huang, and the company (and probably the AI industry as a whole) would likely face years of uncertainty without his vision.

Moreover, Huang's position in the company is likely to be solidified by recent events. Amid the ongoing investigations, investors had to face the possibility of an Nvidia without Huang, and despite the circular financing concerns, they did not like what that looked like.

Ultimately, Huang is unlikely to be forced out again unless the findings of those inquiries leave the company with no choice but to remove him. Consequently, shareholders who held the semiconductor stock throughout the turmoil have been and probably will continue to be rewarded.

#3038. The Stock Market Just Fell 10% From The Highs. Here’s Exactly What I’m Doing With My Own Money.

I’ve invested through plenty of downturns since 2003, and the lessons from the last big one are guiding what I’m doing now.

By Matt Frankel, CFP® – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:12PM EST

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average both fell 10% from their record closes last Friday, putting them in correction territory. At the end of last week, the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 had fallen about 18% from its peak and is approaching a bear market, typically defined as a 20% decline. Most of the damage has come from a sharp reversal in AI stocks, and the past couple of weeks have included Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as Nvidia's (NVDA +31.48%) CEO and an 11% drop in Anthropic (ANT -1.43%) shares on its second day of trading. Then, Huang was reinstated on Monday morning, causing even more volatility (but to the upside).

I'm a Certified Financial Planner®. I've been investing since 2003, and I've lived through the financial crisis, the COVID-19 crash, and the 2022 bear market, among others. With that in mind, here's what I'm doing with my own money right now, and just as importantly, what I'm not doing.

First, I'm not dumping stocks or moving my portfolio to cash. By the time things feel calmer, prices have already recovered. I personally know a lot of people who regret bailing out of the stock market in 2008 due to panic.

It also helps to remember how common corrections are. The S&P 500 has gone through about 38 corrections and 14 bear markets since 1950, and every one of them eventually recovered. The index has had an average intra-year decline of about 14% in every year since 1980, yet its average calendar-year return over that span was positive 13.3%. In other words, drops like this one are the price of admission for long-term stock market returns.

Warren Buffett once said to "be greedy when others are fearful." And while I didn't do that during the financial crisis (I was a graduate student at the time with little money to invest), how I handled it in 2020 is one of my proudest moments to look back on as an investor.

The COVID-19 crash initially caused most stocks to plunge, but it hit real estate investment trusts (REITs) especially hard. Hotels sat empty, malls were shut down, and movie theaters went dark, and some investors openly questioned whether these businesses would survive. That's when I took a deep breath and bought shares of Ryman Hospitality Properties (RHP +1.68%), Simon Property Group (SPG +1.21%), Tanger Factory Outlets (SKT +1.99%), and EPR Properties (EPR +1.88%).

It was a nerve-wracking time to buy, but I kept asking myself whether these well-run companies, with valuable properties and solid balance sheets, would still be standing in five years. I believed they would. Well, Ryman has gone up roughly tenfold from its 2020 lows, and the others have delivered excellent returns as well. The lesson I took away is that some of the best opportunities show up when the headlines are at their worst.

Having said all that, I'm not just sitting on my hands. I'm actively looking for discounted opportunities, especially in AI stocks, since most of the selling has been concentrated there.

What stands out to me is the gap between how AI stocks are trading and how AI businesses are performing. Nvidia just reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. Yet heading into that report, the stock traded for about 13 times forward earnings, below the S&P 500's multiple of about 18. Alphabet's (GOOGL +6.34%) Google Cloud more than doubled its revenue in the third quarter, and its backlog reached $561 billion.

Alphabet (GOOG +5.88%), Oracle (ORCL +12.34%), and Forgent Power (NYSE: FPS), all of which I already own, are at the top of my list. I'm also keeping an eye on stocks like Marvell Technology (MRVL +18.37%), KLA (KLAC +14.96%), and Sterling Infrastructure (STRL +12.44%). Of course, I have no idea where the bottom is, so I plan to buy in stages over the coming weeks and months.

Finally, I'm not touching my emergency fund to buy stocks, no matter how cheap they look. Any money I might need over the next few years stays out of the stock market, which is what allows me to ride out drops like this one without being forced to sell at a bad time.

Nobody knows whether this correction will turn into a bear market or how long it will last. To be clear, if I buy any of these stocks in the near future, it's entirely possible that I'll be "too early." And that's OK. I didn't hit any of the real estate stocks at their exact bottoms in 2020, and I'm not trying to time it this time either. But I'm confident that five years from now, I'll be glad I used this sell-off to add to great businesses at lower prices. That's what happened in 2020, and I think it's a good bet that it will happen again.

When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. After all, Stock Advisor's total average return is 719%* — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 192% for the S&P 500.

Grok AI is being sued over disturbing deepfake images and we're not surprised

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Elon Musk's company is facing two new lawsuits over its image-generation capabilities, raising serious questions about what happens when powerful AI tools can manipulate photographs of real people without their permission.

Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX, the parent company of Grok developer xAI and social media platform X. Both states allege that the company failed to implement adequate safeguards against the creation of nonconsensual sexual images, including child sexual abuse material.

According to Reuters, these are the first lawsuits brought by U.S. states over the controversy, although several attorneys general have already investigated Grok's image-generation features.

The lawsuits also raise a broader concern for anyone who shares photos online. As AI image generators become more realistic and accessible, how much control do people actually have over what others can create using their pictures?

Here's what happened, what the lawsuits allege and what it could mean for Grok users.

The lawsuits focus on Grok's ability to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

Grok includes image-generation and editing features that can transform an uploaded photo using text instructions. According to the states, users exploited these capabilities to create explicit or partially nude images of real people without their knowledge or consent.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The complaints specifically point to Grok's controversial "spicy mode," which the states say enabled the generation of sexual content without sufficient protections.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield argue that the company promoted the safety of its tools while failing to prevent the creation and distribution of harmful images.

The states accuse SpaceX of violating consumer protection laws and are seeking financial penalties, damages and court orders requiring the company to stop the alleged violations.

These are allegations in civil lawsuits, not findings of wrongdoing by a court.

One of the most alarming figures cited in the lawsuits comes from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH).

The organization estimated that between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok generated and posted approximately 3 million sexualized images on X, including around 23,000 images that appeared to depict children.

That works out to roughly 190 sexualized images every minute over the study period.

The figures are estimates from the organization's research rather than a confirmed count of illegal images. Nevertheless, the scale described in the study has become a central part of the states' allegations.

The Virginia Attorney General's Office also alleges that nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified in the study remained publicly accessible on X at least a week after they were identified.

Yes. In January 2026, xAI announced restrictions on Grok's image-editing capabilities, including measures intended to prevent users from generating images of real people in revealing clothing where doing so would be illegal.

However, subsequent reporting raised questions about whether the changes were effective.

In February, Reuters found that Grok could still generate sexualized images of people even when prompts explicitly stated that the subjects had not consented.

The new lawsuits argue that the company's safeguards were inadequate and that its public assurances about user safety were misleading. The company has separately taken legal action against individuals it alleges misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

For most users, the concern goes beyond generating inappropriate AI images.

The lawsuits highlight a growing problem with generative AI: someone may be able to use a photograph of another person to produce realistic fabricated content without that person's permission.

An AI-generated image does not have to depict something that actually happened to cause harm. A convincing fake can be copied, shared or used to harass someone, especially when it circulates on a major social media platform.

The risk is particularly concerning for parents whose children's photos may be publicly accessible online. These lawsuits do not mean that every Grok user has had their photos manipulated, nor do they establish that simply uploading a photo to X causes Grok to generate an explicit image.

Still, they are a reminder that publicly available images can be vulnerable to misuse by people with access to powerful AI editing tools.

Users concerned about this risk can review the visibility of their social media accounts, limit public sharing of sensitive images and report manipulated content when they encounter it. Such precautions cannot eliminate the possibility of misuse, especially when a photograph has already been copied or circulated elsewhere.

Both states are seeking penalties and court orders aimed at stopping the alleged unlawful conduct. The courts have not yet determined whether SpaceX violated either state's consumer protection laws.

The company also faces more than a dozen lawsuits from individuals who allege that Grok was used to create nonconsensual sexual images of them.

The outcome of the lawsuit could help determine how much responsibility AI companies bear when their tools are used to create harmful images of real people.

But for now, the Grok lawsuits underscore a concern that extends to AI image generation as it has become remarkably powerful, but protecting the people whose likenesses appear in those images remains an unresolved challenge.

#3036. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

#3035. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.

#3034. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.

#3031. These Seniors Will Get Their First Social Security Check With the 2027 COLA in December, But Most Others Will Have to Wait

Only a few more weeks are standing between you and higher Social Security benefits.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:15PM EST

If you've been struggling with your retirement expenses, the 2027 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) probably can't come soon enough. This will boost everyone's benefit by 3.6%, adding roughly $75 per month to the average check.

Though the COLA will be applied to the December 2026 payment, benefits usually go out in the month after they're due, so most won't see an increase to their checks until January. However, a small group of seniors will receive their benefit increase in December.

The Social Security Administration follows a strict payment schedule in which most people receive their checks on the second, third, or fourth Wednesday of the month, depending on their birthday. The later your birthday falls in the month, the later your checks arrive.

But there are a couple of groups who don't follow this rule. Seniors who began claiming Social Security prior to May 1997 and those on Supplemental Security Income (SSI) usually receive their Social Security checks on the third of the month, regardless of their birthday.

In most months, this isn't an issue, but sometimes the third falls on a weekend. In that case, payments go out on the last business day before the third. And that's what's happening with the first checks that include the 2027 Social Security COLA.

Jan. 3, 2027, is a Sunday, so it's not an eligible payment day. The weekday before that is Jan. 1, 2027, which is a federal holiday, so payments won't go out then either. Instead, older beneficiaries and those on SSI will get their first Social Security checks with the COLA on Dec. 31, 2026.

It's not much earlier, but it could be a big help to some seniors, especially those struggling with holiday costs. Just bear in mind that, if you fall into this group, you won't get another Social Security check until Feb. 3, 2027, so make sure you're budgeting carefully to stretch your check until then.

If you're not on SSI, your payments will go out on either the second, third, or fourth Wednesday in January, as follows:

This schedule should be familiar to you if you've already been on Social Security for a while. If you've just signed up recently or plan to start receiving checks next year, mark the appropriate payment date on your calendar and check your bank account on that day to make sure your new check arrived as scheduled.

#3024. 3 AI Stocks Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller Has Been Quietly Buying

Druckenmiller started new positions in SpaceX, Palantir, and AppLovin in Q3.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

Billionaire hedge fund manager Stanley Druckenmiller has seemingly turned bearish on stocks, saying recently at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin that he was largely sitting out of the market and just looking to "not lose money."

However, while he was a net seller of stocks in Q3, he was quietly adding new positions in three artificial intelligence stocks: Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.35%), Palantir Technologies (PLTR +11.06%), and AppLovin (APP +7.36%).

Let's look at what may have attracted Druckenmiller to these three AI stocks.

Space Exploration Technologies — or SpaceX — is an exciting stock, with the potential to disrupt multiple industries and see rapid growth. While CEO Elon Musk has made some pretty fanciful predictions, such as the company eventually becoming worth more than Earth itself, that hyperbole doesn't take away from what is ultimately a huge opportunity.

The company’s biggest advantage at this time is its reusable rocket technology, which it has been testing with its much larger-payload Starship.

With the company recently catching the upper stage of Starship, it has now demonstrated that it can recapture both stages of the rocket, positioning it for the beginning of rapid rocket reuse. That would completely turn the economics of space on its head and give SpaceX an enormous cost advantage not only for launching more Starlink satellites but also for the future launch of orbital data centers.

In the interim, SpaceX should see significant growth in its terrestrial AI infrastructure business, where it is achieving strong payback periods and growing rapidly. Meanwhile, it also looks as if it wants to take aim at the U.S. mobile market with its Starlink satellite service, and its Cursor AI platform is also growing quickly.

While Druckenmiller was busy selling down positions in hardware companies, he said at the conference that investors should focus on the AI application layer. As such, perhaps it should be no surprise that he was adding shares of Palantir to his portfolio.

Palantir has become the ultimate AI-applications-layer stock, with its AI platform almost akin to an AI operating system. The company has been seeing rapid growth as customers adopt its platform to make AI models more useful in the real world.

Its platform does this by gathering information from a variety of sources and populating an ontology that it then links to physical assets, business processes, and concepts. This significantly reduces potential AI hallucinations and puts guardrails in place to help AI models perform at their best.

The strength of the company's business can be seen not just in its rapid revenue growth but also in the significant growth it's seeing with existing customers. Over the past 12 months, the company's net dollar retention was an astonishing 165%, which essentially means clients who have been with the company for over a year increased their spending with Palantir by an average of 65%, net of any churn or contraction.

To me, there is no better testament to how good the company's solution is than this metric.

AppLovin is another company benefiting from using AI to drive growth. The company is primarily an adtech solutions provider to the mobile gaming industry, and it has seen rapid revenue growth and margin expansion since the launch of its Axon-2 solution in 2023.

The stock was beaten down following a slight earnings miss in Q2, as its model didn't improve at its typical rate, but the company bounced back in Q3, with revenue surging 55%. Meanwhile, it sees the transition to a new model that performs better than past ones with less data as a key future driver, as it helps it reach newer customers and verticals.

Given AppLovin's growth and valuation (it has a forward P/E of just 19 times), it's easy to see what Druckenmiller likes about the stock.

Reacting to the Q2 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reiterated a buy rating on NVDA and increased his price target to $300 from $288. "This is our Top Pick in the semis group, with a compelling product cycle, exceptional growth and valuation below peers," said the 5-star analyst.

#3021. Nvidia Soared 35% on Jensen Huang's Return. Is It Too Late to Buy?

The stock is still down with room to run.

By John Bromels – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:31PM EST

If you've been following the fast-moving Jensen Huang drama at Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%), you probably have a severe case of whiplash this morning. Nvidia announced today that its board unanimously voted to reinstate the former CEO less than two weeks after his resignation.

In response, Nvidia's shares jumped as much as 35% intraday after falling 47.5% from their early October highs.

Given the size of the jump, is it too late to buy Nvidia stock? I don't think so. Here's why.

The Jensen Huang soap opera -- which includes reports of foreign spies, lurid affairs, and shocking reversals of fortune -- is hard to look away from. Indeed, it's easily the most exciting drama to hit the stock market in years. But it's the kind of drama that doesn't tend to impact long-term results.

No, it's never a good thing when your CEO's name is plastered all over the news as having had an affair with a potential foreign spy, but unless there are ongoing national security implications for the company, the business should keep chugging along regardless.

And chug along it has. Nvidia's Q3 revenue hit $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year (YOY), and up 20% from the prior quarter. Meanwhile, data center revenue totaled $107.6 billion, up 110% year over year. Gross margins stayed close to 75%. Net income more than doubled YOY to $65.3 billion, while management guided for about $130 billion in Q4 revenue (which would be a 91% year-over-year increase).

That Q4 projection, it's worth noting, was made by CFO Colette Kress after Huang's resignation and prior to his reinstatement. It seems unlikely that Huang's return would result in lower projections. If anything, the sense that Nvidia has put its drama behind it might only improve its outlook.

But is the drama actually in Nvidia's rearview mirror?

Various figures within the Trump administration, including the president himself, publicly backed Huang prior to today's surprise reinstatement.

Afterward, Trump took credit for the reinstatement, telling CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia's board and given them "assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot," reiterating that, in his view, Huang "did nothing wrong."

If Nvidia's board was concerned that national security risks or consequences tied to Huang's personal behavior or business activities could blow back on the company as a whole, it's unlikely they would have unanimously approved his return.

Last week, the board created a national security and export control oversight committee, with an independent investigation ongoing, so investors can't quite regard the matter as fully closed.

Nvidia's growth comes from a product lineup, supply chain, and customer relationships built by thousands of people over many years. There was never a good reason to expect that growth to flag without Huang aboard. Still, his return should soothe a nervous market.

Even after the 35% post-reinstatement surge, Nvidia's stock is still down about 11% for the year, despite quarter after quarter of strong results. That gap suggests the market has been pricing in more worry than the fundamentals warrant. In my view, there's still plenty of room for shares to run.

#3020. Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me

In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.

Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”

Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

#3018. Is the Worst Over for Nvidia Stock?

Raised guidance helped ease investor fears even before Huang's return.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:33PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA +31.48%) calmed some investor fears by raising fiscal 2028 guidance following the departure of founder and CEO Jensen Huang. However, the strong Nov. 17 report and fiscal 2028 forecast don't necessarily mean the worst is over for the stock, as longer-term worries persist, even with Huang unexpectedly being reinstated as CEO on Monday morning.

Let's dig into Nvidia's fiscal third-quarter results and prospects to see whether the semiconductor stock is a buy.

The biggest recent news for Nvidia came after the quarterly report, when Huang was welcomed back. Before that, the company had raised its revenue forecast for next year from 70% growth to 75% growth due to increased confidence in both supply and demand. There had been a growing concern that the company would reduce its forecast as it tries to flush out sales that eventually make their way to China illegally, so this was a big relief.

Showing confidence in the stock and business, Nvidia said it plans to repurchase $227 billion worth of shares by the end of fiscal 2028. Meanwhile, then-interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress was peppered with questions concerning everything from increased competition to margins and pricing power to neocloud financing to export controls and a potential data center slowdown in 2028.

While Kress handled these questions well, they are unlikely to go away. In the meantime, as competitors start to catch up and artificial intelligence (AI) models ironically weaken Nvidia's CUDA moat, the company's biggest strength is availability, having locked up scarce components, like high bandwidth memory (HBM) and fab capacity. This will continue to fuel results next fiscal year but could erode over time.

As for the quarterly results themselves, they were once again spectacular. Nvidia's Q3 revenue soared 103% to $115.8 billion, well above the $109.1 billion analyst consensus. Adjusted earnings per share (EPS), meanwhile, skyrocketed 111% to $2.68 from $1.27, coming in above analyst estimates of $2.48.

Data center segment revenue once again led the way, up 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Nvidia's smaller edge computing segment, meanwhile, saw revenue jump 42% to $8.2 billion.

Within its data center segment, hyperscaler revenue climbed 71% to $60.1 billion, helped by the ramp-up of its Vera Rubin platform. AI cloud, industrial, and enterprise (ACIE) revenue surged 195% to $47.5 billion. The company said the growth was driven by the start of Vera Rubin shipments to neocloud customers and AI labs starting to build their own data centers.

One of the big drivers for Nvidia in the coming year will be the continued ramp-up of Vera Rubin. The platform contributed $20 billion in revenue in the quarter, which it said was the fastest product ramp in its history. With Vera Rubin costing about $40 billion per gigawatt of compute capacity versus $25 billion for Blackwell, Nvidia gets a very nice price lift as customers move to its newest system.

The company continues to generate a huge amount of cash, with operating cash flow of $48.3 billion and free cash flow of $28.1 billion in the quarter. It ended the period with cash and marketable securities of $53.5 billion and $32.3 billion in debt. It also has $65.5 billion in non-marketable securities, which are its investments in non-public companies, and $44.2 billion in marketable equity securities, which are investments in public companies.

Looking ahead, Nvidia guided for fiscal Q4 revenue to come in around $130 billion, which would represent 91% growth.

Nvidia is growing rapidly, and the stock is cheap, trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio below 10 times analyst estimates for fiscal 2028 earnings. The issue is what comes next.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

Application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which are custom AI chips, and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +6.85%) graphics processing units (GPUs) are catching up and, in some cases, outperforming Nvidia's GPUs on a price-to-performance basis. Meanwhile, Anthropic's (ANT -1.43%) Claude Mythos model just made it a whole lot easier to have models run on other chips. While Nvidia’s supply chain advantages will protect it in the near-to-medium term, there could be a serious risk of future price erosion and margin compression.

As such, despite the quarterly report and Huang’s return easing some immediate concerns, I'd stay on the sidelines for now.

While the first Googlebooks on the market have received mixed reviews, these features could help the laptops gain more useful features in Chrome that other browsers already offer.

Also: Googlebooks? The best laptop for Android users is something else

If you’ve ever had to share your screen on a video call, you know how irritating it can be to switch tabs without having to repeatedly start and stop sharing. Also: 6 Chrome default settings I changed to instantly

When you hover over a collapsed vertical tab rail with your mouse or trackpad, it will expand, so you can read full tab titles, switch tabs, or manage groups. The rail will collapse again when you move the cursor away.

The Chrome update allows you to manually resize your vertical tab bar to view longer page titles when needed. The browser will remember your custom tab width, even after you open a new window or restart the browser. (You’ll just need to turn “Auto expand tabs on hover” off for it to work.)

Also: Google Chrome running slow? 5 easy ways to speed it up fast

Outside of these new features, a few of Chrome M157’s performance fixes include the ability to press Ctrl+L to reveal and select web addresses; keeping your bookmarks bar visible in fullscreen mode and while screen sharing; better media controls while using Picture-in-Picture mode; and the ability to partially translate PDFs within your browser.

If you have Chrome set up to automatically download and install updates, you won’t have to lift a finger to take advantage of the new features and performance boosts.

But if you’ve disabled automatic updates, you can manually update by selecting the three-dot menu in the top-right corner of your Chrome window and navigating to Help > About Google Chrome > Relaunch.

Also: My week with new Googlebooks: The good, the bad, and the promising

If the Relaunch option is greyed out or nowhere to be found, you’re running on the latest version of Chrome. And if you were working on something before the update, don’t worry: Chrome will save your open tabs and reopen them automatically when you restart.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

These settings will keep your data safer than the default settings.

Luckily, you can mitigate or even eliminate the amount of data Claude knows about you, as long as you know where to look.

By default, most AI chatbots have a setting on by default that allows them to be trained on the conversations you have. This is the first and likely the most important setting you need to disable. Here’s how to turn it off.

The settings essentially remain the same across web, iOS and Android:

You may not see this option because with some accounts, like Enterprise plans, Claude doesn’t automatically collect this data. So if you have a Claude account through work, you might not have to worry about this.

While you’re at it, if you’re a Claude Code user, these settings will let you delete Code sessions stored on Anthropic’s server without deleting local sessions on your computer.

If you’ve ever shared a chat with anyone, you can also delete those chats in this menu as well.

Read More: Keep Your Data Yours: How to Opt Out of AI Chatbot Training

Anthropic will use your location when using Claude to “improve product experience.” It will use your device’s IP address to identify your city and region, but you can disable this setting — to some extent. How you go about doing this will depend on what device you’re using to access Claude.

According to the support article, if you’re using the mobile app (iOS or Android) or the web extension, the location settings are located within the device’s settings and not the Claude app settings. However, I found two ways to do this on Android. (See below.)

The Claude app will not request access to your location unless your prompt has a specific location-based query, like “What are some of the best sushi restaurants around me?” Only then will the app request permission.

However, if you already have given Claude access on Android or iOS, here’s how you can revoke permission.

I was surprised to see a section in the Settings of the Android app that I didn’t see on iOS, but it will also allow you to disable your location right from the app.

One thing to keep in mind is that turning your location off can affect features like searches that require your location, but Anthropic explicitly states that it collects your IP address to infer coarse-grained location to ensure usage of Claude complies with its terms and to prevent abuse — despite questionable allegations.

Like other AI chatbots, Claude has built-in “memory” so it can more easily have context about your conversations. Memory is on by default: The chatbot will remember personal preferences and other information and will be able to take that into consideration in other conversations, even if you don’t explicitly mention it in your current session.

If you’d prefer a clean slate, you can ask in the chat what memories it has collected about you and then tell Claude to delete specific memories or all of them. However, there’s a dedicated section in the settings to help you view and manage memories directly.

In the web version of Claude, do the following to access your memory settings:

This will display all stored memories Claude has for you. You can edit a specific memory to your liking by clicking on the pencil icon on the right side of the memory or delete it entirely by clicking on the trash icon.

To prevent Claude from creating new memories from your conversations:

If you have had conversations with Claude that were sensitive in nature and still had the “Help improve our AI models” option enabled, odds are that Anthropic has already trained Claude on that conversation. There’s no way to change that.

However, you should find those conversations in your chat history and delete them. After you’ve done that and disabled AI training on your conversations, you should opt for incognito mode for any further sensitive conversations you might want to have going forward.

Incognito chats aren’t saved in your history, nor are they used to train models.

#3014. Goodbye, Gemini Gems: How to use Google’s new Skills – and share them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google is retiring Gemini Gems. Here's what to do to access the same tools as Skills.

Google is replacing Gemini Gems with Skills starting Nov. 17, 2026, and it’s carrying over features that let you share Skills and add files from Google products.

Google has announced that it’s turning Gems, a Gemini feature that lets you create customizable AI chatbots, into Skills, which let you create custom instructions for Gemini. Any Gems you have created will automatically convert, but you can transfer them manually if you want to start using them now.

To help with the transition, Google revealed that two Gems features are moving, too: the ability to share creations and to include Drive, Notebook, and Photos files as part of your Skill’s instructions.

While the Gemini Gems feature is technically going away, any Gems you’ve created aren’t.

If you access the Gems portion of Gemini (since the feature is on the way out, you now have to access this through Settings), you’ll see a message that says “Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating all of your Gems to Skills.” (The cutoff date for accessing your Gems will be Dec. 16, 2026. Workspace business, enterprise, and non-profit accounts will get cut off in March 2027, and Workspace education accounts will be cut off in June 2027.)

A Gemini Skill functions much the same as a Gem. You describe specific situations when Gemini should use the Skill automatically and tell Gemini what you want the Skill to do (it’s best to give specific examples of output). Google gives the example of a marketing team sharing a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive, or a team lead sharing an onboarding skill based on the team handbook.

The biggest difference is that Gems were standalone chats, while Skills are custom instructions that work in any conversation.

You can create as many Skills as you want, but only 100 can be active at a time.

To get users familiar with Skills, Google is bringing over two features from Gems.

First, you can now share any Skill with other users. When you share a Skill, you can choose whether the other person has permission to edit or view only. To share a Skill, go to the three-bar menu in the top left > Customize > Skills. You can view or change permissions from that screen.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

When a Skill is added, Gemini can use it automatically, or you can @mention it in chat to trigger it. One small caveat, though: you can only share Skills through the Gemini web app at the moment, not the mobile app.

Additionally, when you’re creating a Gemini Skill, you can choose to include files of up to 100MB from other Google products like Drive, Photos, and Notebook, along with files from your local device. Gemini will reference these files every time the Skill runs and update in real time, Google says. These features existed with Gems; Google is just moving them to Skills to make the new feature more comparable.

#3013. Meta’s Carbon Emissions Went Up 45% Last Year. AI Is Making It Worse

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Meta's 2026 sustainability report isn't a glowing review, thanks to AI.

Meta promised to be carbon-neutral and water-positive by 2030 — that is, the company would offset as much carbon dioxide as it created and return more water to local watersheds than it used. But like every Big Tech company, Meta is sacrificing its climate goals for artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to run it.

In Meta’s 2026 sustainability report, released on Thursday, Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline … We’ll continue to invest in emissions reductions.”

It’s a disappointing, if unsurprising, announcement. Microsoft, Amazon and Google have also all backtracked on their climate goals in their rush to build hyperscale data centers, the turbocharged server farms needed to keep AI online. Microsoft’s president, Brad Smith, said in 2023 that the company’s net zero goal was “before the explosion in artificial intelligence.”

Meta’s net emissions in 2025 were 11.8 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a 45% increase year over year, the company says. Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are primary drivers of the climate crisis, worsening natural disasters, causing more extreme weather patterns and disrupting the lives of everyone and everything on the planet.

Take one of Meta’s Louisiana data centers, Hyperion, for example. CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the behemoth in 2025, showing how the facility is nearly the size of Manhattan. When it comes online in 2030, it’s expected to create two gigawatts of capacity for AI, with the ability to scale in the future. But it also requires equally massive demands on the state’s energy grid.

Meta details in length its strategies for mitigating the environmental impact of its work, including improved water-use efficiencies in its data centers and approximately 77% less embodied carbon in its new data center designs compared to its original ones.

But, again, AI has made an indelible mark on those efforts. The company also reports that its electricity consumption “increased 35% year over year as additional data centers came online.”

Meta wrote that “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.” Arguably, as one of the biggest hyperscalers driving the buildout of AI infrastructure here in the US and abroad, Meta should have known.

#3012. Is AMD's Stock in Trouble After a Concerning Short-Seller Report?

A recent short-seller report called into question AMD's high exposure to China.

By David Jagielski, CPA – Nov 23, 2026 at 3:36PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

A short-seller report can be devastating for a stock. Even if it's untrue or full of misinformation, it can strike fear into investors and send a stock reeling.

Last week, shares of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +6.85%) fell amid a short-seller report, which called into question its ties to a Chinese company, IEIT Systems. Ties to China are a sensitive issue in light of Nvidia's recent controversy involving CEO Jensen Huang and a possible spy. That led Huang to resign from the company, although he would end up being reinstated.

AMD is up big this year, but does this short-seller report give investors reason to dump the stock before it's too late?

Hunterbrook Media, which has a short position in AMD and thus stands to benefit from its decline in price, claims that the tech company "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong." It also states that a blacklisted Chinese company, IEIT Systems, has been gaining access to newer AMD firmware, which is needed to run AMD’s chips.

AMD has dismissed the allegations of any wrongdoing, stating that it is in compliance with U.S. export laws, which impose significant restrictions on the type of chips and technology that can be sent to China.

The key, however, is whether any products were sold to Chinese customers that violated U.S. export law, and as long as that hasn't been the case, and at this point there's no reason to believe it is, then there's no reason for investors to worry about references to Chinese customers.

AMD's revenue totaled $34.6 billion in its most recent fiscal year, and of that tally, more than 22% was related to customers in China (including Hong Kong). Sales to China aren't on their own a reason for investors to worry about AMD's stock.

AMD's stock has been falling in recent weeks, and it's now down more than 30% from its 52-week high of over $658. The stock, however, isn't cheap, trading at close to 100 times its trailing earnings.

At a time when market conditions may not be ideal for the tech sector, with interest rates potentially rising higher next month, there could be more bearish activity ahead for AMD and the broader tech market.

For investors who are willing to hang on for the long haul (e.g., five-plus years), AMD may be worth buying given its strong position in the chip market. In the short run, however, this could be a risky stock to own, as there may be plenty of room for it to fall lower given its high price tag today.

#3011. Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Microsoft announced two new AI models at Ignite 2026 that promise impressive performance for much lower cost. They could reshape its relationship with OpenAI and Anthropic for good.

At today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the company introduced two new frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Microsoft says MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

This doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also important to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the company paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As users adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous

There’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

This becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

Think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a company is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the new models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open issue.

The company also described clearly that these new models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Encryption can't protect your messages from an AI agent peeking over your shoulder.

Don’t ask your AI agent to read and decipher that lengthy text message. And don’t screenshot it either. It may seem harmless, but Signal’s latest setting underlines that it isn’t.

Whittaker said that this isn’t the first time Signal has taken such measures against an operating system. Last year, it blocked screenshots of Signal messages from Microsoft’s Recall AI on Windows 11.

Now the company is taking a similar approach to Apple’s iOS 27 and Android operating systems, where AI assistants try to read your Signal screen.

The problem is the same for the three major OS companies. Microsoft, Google and Apple are incorporating AI into their operating systems, and Signal says that compromises the space for third-party developers, including Signal, to build apps for these systems.

Whittaker said the screenshot setting won’t fix everything, because AI agents can still sneakily access data on your phone. Tech companies should take steps to give developers more choice, such as an opt-out to disable AI agent access, and provide more documentation on how big tech AI agents work.

“Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience,” Whittaker said. “This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on MacOS.”

In most cases, text messages are encrypted when they travel between devices. But AI agents can bypass that. John Strand, CEO of Black Hills Information Security, explained that when you access the information, it has to be decrypted because you cannot read encrypted data.

“So, if an AI agent can access screenshots or directly observe what’s happening on your screen, it can read those messages without ever having to break the encryption itself,” said Strand. “That’s the scary part. You can have incredibly strong encryption, but if something can see what the user sees, that encryption isn’t going to protect you at that point.”

If you want to take screenshots in Signal, you can disable the setting, but that could mean AI agents could access you and your senders’ information, like text messages and shared files such as photos.

Strand said the worst-case scenario is that an attacker could see everything you see, from private conversations to passwords. And that’s what Signal is trying to avoid.

“They want to make sure that if something like this happens, they’ve done absolutely everything they reasonably can to protect their customers and the information being accessed through their application,” Strand said.

Signal, Apple and Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
